adventures.name: Bobcat Arrow of Light
adventures.summary: Start your trail! Team up with Scouts, learn the Oath and Law, and visit a Scout troop.

requirements.adultText: Show how a patrol works by picking a team name and voting in a patrol leader. Then talk together about why small Scout teams get things done.
requirements.kidText: A patrol is a small team of Scouts. Pick a team name and vote for a leader. Then talk about why teams work well.

lines: A patrol is a small team of Scouts, like your den.
Patrols pick a name and vote for a leader.
Everyone in a patrol gets a job to do.
One Scout might read the map. Another packs the first-aid kit.
Scouts make the choices. Adults only help.
Small teams get more done, and everyone gets a say.

params.title: Form Your Patrol
kidSteps: Meet with your patrol. That is your den or small Scout team.
Brainstorm patrol names and pick one.
Vote for a patrol leader.
Talk about why small teams work well.
params.parentNote: Check that your Scout joined in picking the name and holding the vote, and can give one reason the patrol method works, such as sharing jobs and taking turns leading.

questions.prompt: What is a patrol?
choices: A small team of Scouts working together
questions.explain: A patrol is a small team that plans and does things together.

questions.prompt: Why do Scouts work in patrols?
choices: Everyone gets a job and a say
questions.explain: Patrols let Scouts take turns leading, share jobs, and learn from each other.

requirements.adultText: Spend time getting to know the other Scouts in your patrol. A question toss, a compliment circle, or making a patrol flag are all good ways to do it.
requirements.kidText: Get to know your patrol, your small Scout team! Try a beach ball question toss, a patrol flag, or a compliment circle. In a compliment circle, you say nice things about each other.

params.title: Meet Your Patrol
kidSteps: Pick one: a beach ball question toss, a compliment circle, or a patrol flag.
Do it with your patrol.
Learn one new thing about each Scout.
params.parentNote: Look for your Scout joining in and being able to share something new they learned about another Scout.

requirements.adultText: Know the Scout Oath by heart. Reciting it aloud with the patrol still happens in person.
requirements.kidText: The Scout Oath is a promise every Scout makes. Put the lines in the right order. Then say it out loud!

lines: The Scout Oath is a promise every Scout makes out loud.
It starts: On my honor I will do my best.
Next, do your duty to God and country. A duty is a job you promise to do.
Then obey the Scout Law and help other people at all times.
Last, keep yourself physically strong, mentally awake, and morally straight.
That means a strong body, a sharp mind, and doing what is right.

params.prompt: Put the Scout Oath in order.
steps: On my honor I will do my best
To do my duty to God and my country
and to obey the Scout Law;
To help other people at all times;
To keep myself physically strong,
mentally awake,
and morally straight.

requirements.notes: Sub-item of official requirement 3 (recite the Oath and Law with your patrol). In-game this is rehearsal; steps are the Oath split at its natural pauses.

requirements.adultText: Know the twelve points of the Scout Law and what each one means. Reciting with the patrol still happens in person.
requirements.kidText: The Scout Law has 12 points. Each point tells how a Scout acts. Show what you know about them!

lines: The Scout Law has 12 points. Each one is a way Scouts act.
The first point is trustworthy. The last point is reverent.
Trustworthy means you tell the truth and keep your promises.
Thrifty means you use time, food, and supplies wisely. You do not waste them.
Brave does not mean you never feel scared. It means you do right anyway.
Example: you feel nervous but still tell the truth. That is brave.

questions.prompt: How many points are in the Scout Law?
questions.explain: There are 12 points, from trustworthy to reverent.

questions.prompt: Which point means you tell the truth and keep your promises?
questions.explain: Trustworthy means people can count on you.

questions.prompt: A Scout is thrifty. What does that mean?
choices: Use time, food, and supplies wisely
questions.explain: Thrifty means you do not waste things, and you work to pay your own way.

questions.prompt: A Scout is brave. Which is an example?
choices: Doing the right thing even when you feel afraid
Taking a dare to look tough
questions.explain: Brave does not mean no fear. It means doing what is right anyway.

requirements.notes: Sub-item of official requirement 3. Quiz covers a sample of the 12 points; implementers may add more questions later.

requirements.adultText: With your patrol, write a Code of Conduct: a short list of rules the group agrees on for how everyone will treat each other and act at meetings and outings.
requirements.kidText: A Code of Conduct is a list of rules your Scout team agrees on. Write one together. Make it fair for everyone.

params.title: Write Your Code of Conduct
kidSteps: Gather your team.
Talk about how Scouts should act at meetings and on trips.
Write a short list of rules everyone agrees on.
Everyone signs or says yes to the code.
params.parentNote: Look for rules the Scouts came up with themselves and for every Scout agreeing. Keep a copy somewhere the patrol will see it, such as a poster.

requirements.adultText: Show how to give the Scouts BSA sign and salute and how to shake hands the Scout way, and explain when each is used. These replace the Cub Scout versions.
requirements.kidText: Scouts have a sign, a salute, and a handshake. Learn them in the game first. Then show each one to your leader.

lines: Scouts shake hands with the left hand. Try it when you meet a Scout!
For the Scout sign, hold up three fingers. Your thumb holds down your little finger.
The three fingers stand for the three parts of the Scout Oath.
Those are your duties, or jobs you promise: God and country, others, and self.
For the salute, raise your sign hand to your head.
Your pointer finger touches the hat brim or your right eyebrow.

params.title: Show Your Scout Signs
kidSteps: Make the Scout sign: right hand up, three fingers raised, thumb over little finger.
Do the salute: bring the sign hand to your eyebrow or hat brim.
Shake hands with your left hand.
Explain when you use each one.
params.parentNote: Sign: right arm to shoulder height, elbow bent, thumb over the little fingernail, three fingers up. Salute: touch the forefinger to the hat brim or right eyebrow. Handshake: left hand.

questions.prompt: Which hand do Scouts use to shake hands?
questions.explain: The Scout handshake is done with the left hand.

questions.prompt: What do the three fingers of the Scout sign stand for?
choices: The three parts of the Scout Oath
questions.explain: They stand for duty to God and country, duty to others, and duty to self.

questions.prompt: Where does your hand go for the Scout salute?
questions.explain: Your pointer finger touches the hat brim or the tip of your right eyebrow.

requirements.adultText: Know the slogan and motto that Scouts BSA uses and how each one guides a Scout.
requirements.kidText: A slogan and a motto are short sayings. Scouts have one of each. Let us see if you know them!

lines: Scouts have a motto and a slogan. Each is a short saying.
The motto is Be Prepared. That means be ready before trouble comes.
The slogan is Do a Good Turn Daily. A slogan tells you what to do.
A good turn is a kind thing you do without being asked.
You do not wait to be paid or thanked.
Example: carry a neighbor's groceries, just to be nice.

questions.prompt: What is the Scout slogan?
questions.explain: The slogan is "Do a Good Turn Daily."

questions.prompt: What is the Scout motto?
questions.explain: The motto is "Be Prepared."

questions.prompt: Which one is a good turn?
choices: Waiting to be paid before you help
questions.explain: A good turn is a kind act you do without asking for a reward.

requirements.adultText: Go see a Scouting America troop in action, either together with fellow patrol members or alongside a parent or guardian. A meeting, a daytime activity, or an overnight each counts.
requirements.kidText: A troop is a group of older Scouts. You will join one soon. Visit a troop meeting or outing to see what it is like.

params.title: Visit a Troop
kidSteps: Ask your parent or leader to set up a troop visit.
Go to a troop meeting, a day outing, or an overnight trip.
Notice how Scouts lead their own meetings.
Ask one Scout what they like best about the troop.
params.parentNote: Your den leader or local council can help you find a troop. The official options are a troop meeting, a daytime activity, or an overnight. Overnights follow Arrow of Light camping rules.

requirements.adultText: At home, a parent or guardian and the Scout work through the exercises in the Scouting America youth protection booklet for parents. Parents should read it first.
requirements.kidText: This one is just for you and your parent at home. You will work through a booklet about staying safe. Ask any question you want.

params.title: Staying Safe at Home
kidSteps: Pick a calm time at home with your parent or guardian.
Do the booklet exercises together.
Ask any questions you have.
Remember: tell a trusted adult if anything ever feels wrong.
params.parentNote: Booklet: "How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent's Guide" (found at the front of the Arrow of Light handbook; online and Spanish versions exist). Read it first, then do the exercises together in a private, calm setting. This is done at home, not as a group.

adventures.name: Personal Fitness
adventures.summary: Plan a camp meal and track your active days. Move with others and check your health record.

requirements.adultText: Plan a balanced meal suited to a camping trip. Then cook it using the sort of gear you would bring on a campout.
requirements.kidText: A balanced meal has foods from different groups. Plan one for a campout. Then cook it with camp gear.

lines: A balanced meal has foods from five groups.
Protein helps your muscles grow. Bean chili is a good camp protein.
Grains give you energy. Rice, bread, and pasta are grains.
Fruits and vegetables give you vitamins. Think apple slices and carrot sticks.
Dairy is milk and cheese. It helps build strong bones.
Candy, soda, and chips are treats. They do not make a balanced meal.

params.title: Cook a Camp Meal
kidSteps: Plan a meal with protein, grains, fruit, vegetables, and dairy.
Check with your parent about food allergies.
Pack the camp gear you would use to cook.
Cook your meal with an adult helping.
params.parentNote: Check allergies and diet needs first. Cooking with a knife requires the Knife Safety adventure first. Official activity options include a picnic-style meal or a pizza on a campout (which needs a BALOO-trained adult).

requirements.adultText: Think about what physical fitness means for you. Keep a two-week log of every day you get half an hour or more of exercise. Share what you enjoyed and whether you keep the Oath's promise to stay strong.
requirements.kidText: Being fit means your body is strong. For 14 days, write down each day you move for 30 minutes or more. Then share what you found.

lines: Being fit means your body is strong and can keep moving.
You keep a log for 14 days. A log is a list of your active days.
A day counts when you move for 30 minutes or more.
Running, biking, swimming, or playing basketball all count.
Five minutes is too short. All day is more than you need.
The Scout Oath says to keep yourself physically strong. That is the fitness promise.

params.title: 14-Day Fitness Log
kidSteps: Pick fun ways to move, such as running, swimming, or basketball.
Each day, move for 30 minutes or more if you can.
Write each active day in a log for 14 days.
Count your active days.
Tell your family or your team what you enjoyed.
Decide if you are keeping the Scout Oath promise to stay physically strong.
params.parentNote: Use the activity log in the Arrow of Light handbook or any chart. The requirement is to track honestly and talk about it, not to reach a set number of days.

questions.prompt: How long must you move for a day to count in your log?
questions.explain: A day counts when you move for 30 minutes or longer.

questions.prompt: Which part of the Scout Oath is about fitness?
questions.explain: The Oath promises to keep yourself physically strong, mentally awake, and morally straight.

requirements.adultText: Spend half an hour exercising with others: your patrol, younger Scouts, or even one friend. Mix stretching with movement, such as a bike ride or a sport.
requirements.kidText: Get moving with others for 30 minutes. Add stretching and active play. Biking or a sport both work.

lines: Move with others for 30 minutes. Start with a warm-up.
A warm-up gets your muscles ready, so you do not get hurt.
Jumping jacks make a great warm-up.
In the game, tap on every beat. Each tap is one jumping jack.
Finish with a cool-down stretch so your body can calm down.
A bike ride, a sport, or a game all count as active play.

params.title: Active With Friends
kidSteps: Pick your group: your team, a younger den, or one friend.
Warm up with stretches.
Be active for 30 minutes, with a bike ride, a sport, or a game.
Finish with a cool-down stretch.
params.parentNote: If you bike, do an ABC Quick Check first (air, brakes, cranks and chain), wear a helmet, and use an Activity Consent form for a ride away from the usual meeting place.

params.prompt: Warm up with jumping jacks. Tap on every beat.

requirements.adultText: Read through the Scout's Annual Health and Medical Record together with a parent or guardian, then talk about which patrol and pack activities the Scout can take part in.
requirements.kidText: The Annual Health and Medical Record lists your health details. Read it with your parent. Talk about what you can do at Scout events.

params.title: Health Record Chat
kidSteps: Sit down with your parent or guardian and the record.
Read through it together.
Talk about which Scout events you can join.
Tell your leader about anything they should know, such as allergies.
params.parentNote: Look over the current Annual Health and Medical Record form together, update anything that changed, and talk openly about what the Scout can and cannot do at activities.

adventures.name: First Aid
adventures.summary: Learn what to do when someone is hurt. Then build your own first-aid kit.

requirements.adultText: Get a parent or guardian's okay, then view the Protect Yourself Rules video made for Arrow of Light Scouts. It teaches Scouts how to protect themselves.
requirements.kidText: Ask your parent for permission. Then watch the Protect Yourself Rules video together. It teaches you how to stay safe.

params.title: Protect Yourself Rules
kidSteps: Ask your parent or guardian for permission.
Watch the Arrow of Light Protect Yourself Rules video together.
Talk about what you learned.
params.parentNote: Preview the Arrow of Light Protect Yourself Rules video (linked from Scouting America's Youth Protection pages) and watch it with your Scout. Invite questions. A trusted adult is always the right person to tell if something feels unsafe.

requirements.adultText: Describe what to do when you find a person who needs help with an injury: check the scene, stay calm, call for help, and give care.
requirements.kidText: If someone is hurt, you can help. There are four steps, and each one starts with C. Put them in order.

lines: When someone is hurt, stay calm and follow four steps.
Step one, Check: look around. Is the place safe for you?
Step two, Calm: take a breath and think about what is needed.
Step three, Call: call 911, or send someone else to call.
Step four, Care: help the person until help arrives.
Example: a friend falls off a bike. Check for cars first, then help.

params.prompt: Put the steps for helping someone who is hurt in order.
steps: Check that the place is safe for you.
Calm down and think about what is needed.
Call 911, or send someone else to call.
Care for the person until help arrives.

requirements.notes: Uses the four-step version from the First Aid First Response activity. The hurry-cases activity teaches a shorter Check, Call, Care version.

requirements.adultText: Act out the response to each hurry case: stroke, poisoning, stopped breathing, sudden cardiac arrest or a heart attack, and serious bleeding. Use a buddy or a dummy, never real force.
requirements.kidText: Hurry cases are emergencies where every second counts. Learn what to do for each one. Then practice with an adult.

lines: A hurry case is an emergency. Every second counts.
Serious bleeding, a heart attack, and stopped breathing are hurry cases.
A stroke and poisoning are hurry cases too. Call 911 right away for all of them.
Small hurts are not hurry cases, like a scrape or a mosquito bite.
A blister or a mild sunburn is small too. Treat it and watch it.
Not sure? Call 911 and ask for help.

params.title: Hurry Case Practice
kidSteps: Learn the three Cs with your parent or leader: Check, Call, Care.
Practice stopping serious bleeding on a buddy. Press hard with gauze or cloth.
Watch an adult show CPR on a rolled blanket. CPR is pushing on the chest to help the heart. Then try the hand position.
Learn the stroke signs called FAST: face, arm, speech, time.
Act out what to do for poisoning. Call 911 for help.
Show your parent each hurry case in your own words.
params.parentNote: Official practice uses buddy role-play, pressure on a pretend wound, and CPR on a rolled blanket or dummy (30 compressions, then 2 pretend breaths). Never practice real compressions on a person. A trained first aider can guide this. Stroke signs: face drooping, arm weakness, speech trouble, time to call 911.

params.prompt: Is it a hurry case or a small injury?

requirements.adultText: Show the right way to help someone who is choking: five back blows, then five belly thrusts, repeating until the object comes out or help arrives. Practice gently on a buddy.
requirements.kidText: Choking means something is stuck in a person's throat. Learn the back blows and belly thrusts. Practice gently.

lines: Choking means something is stuck in a person's throat.
First, ask if they are choking. Send someone to call 911.
Give five back blows between the shoulder blades.
Then stand behind them and wrap your arms around their waist.
Make a fist above the belly button and cover it with your other hand.
Give five quick thrusts in and up. Repeat until it comes out or help arrives.

params.title: Help a Choking Person
kidSteps: Watch an adult show back blows and belly thrusts.
Say what you do first. Ask if they are choking. Send someone to call 911.
Practice the hand positions on a buddy. Use no real force.
Say each step out loud as you do it.
params.parentNote: Official practice is an adult demo plus gentle buddy practice: five back blows with the heel of the hand, then five abdominal thrusts, alternating until the object comes out, the person passes out, or help arrives. Never use full force.

params.prompt: Put the choking steps in order.
steps: Ask if the person is choking and send someone to call 911.
Give five back blows between the shoulder blades.
Stand behind them and wrap your arms around their waist.
Make a fist above the belly button and cover it with your other hand.
Give five quick thrusts, in and up.
Repeat until the object comes out or help arrives.

requirements.adultText: Show how to care for a person in shock: call 911, lay them down, raise the feet slightly if there are no head, neck, back, hip, or leg injuries, keep them warm, give nothing to eat or drink, and stay.
requirements.kidText: Shock can happen after a bad injury. The body gets weak and cold. You can help while you wait. Learn the steps.

lines: Shock can happen after a bad injury. The person feels weak, cold, and scared.
First, call 911 right away. Then have the person lie on their back.
Raise their feet a little, unless their head, neck, back, hip, or leg is hurt.
Cover them with a sheet if the weather is cool.
Give them nothing to eat or drink.
Stay beside them until help arrives, like with a friend who crashed a bike.

params.title: Treat Shock
kidSteps: Pretend to call 911 right away.
Have your buddy lie on their back.
Raise their feet a little, unless their head, neck, back, hip, or leg is hurt.
Cover them if it is cool. Give no food or drink.
Stay with them until help arrives.
params.parentNote: Practice on a willing adult or buddy lying on a mat. Key points: call 911, lie flat, raise the feet slightly only if no head, neck, back, hip, or leg injury, cover if cool, nothing to eat or drink, stay until help arrives.

params.prompt: Put the steps for treating shock in order.
steps: Call 911 for help right away.
Have the person lie down on their back.
Raise their feet a little, unless their head, neck, back, hip, or leg is hurt.
Cover them with a sheet if the weather is cool.
Give them nothing to eat or drink.
Stay with them until help arrives.

requirements.adultText: Show how to treat nosebleeds, insect and animal bites and stings, burns and scalds, and cuts and scratches. Practice each one at a station with a buddy and clean supplies.
requirements.kidText: Four common injuries need simple care: cuts, burns, bites, and nosebleeds. Learn how to treat each one. Then show a grown-up.

lines: Four small injuries need simple care: cuts, burns, bites, and nosebleeds.
Cuts: wash with soap and water, press with clean gauze, then cover.
Burns: cool the burn in chilly water. Cover it with a loose, clean bandage.
Stings: scrape out a stinger with a card edge. Pull a tick out with tweezers.
Nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, and pinch your nostrils for 10 minutes.
Example: you scrape your knee. Wash it, then cover it.

params.title: Four Common Injuries
kidSteps: Cuts and scratches: wash with soap and water, then cover.
Burns: cool the burn in chilly water, then cover it loosely.
Bites and stings: scrape out a stinger, or pull a tick with tweezers.
Nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, and pinch the nose for 10 minutes.
params.parentNote: For bigger cuts, press directly on the wound and have an adult look at it. Remove a tick by grasping it close to the skin and pulling gently. Call for help if a nosebleed lasts over 15 minutes. Check for allergies before using ointment.

params.prompt: Match each treatment to the injury.

items.label: Press on it with clean gauze
Cover with a loose, clean bandage
Scrape out a stinger with a card edge
Pull a tick out with tweezers

requirements.adultText: Assemble your own first-aid kit, then show what each item is for and the correct way to use it.
requirements.kidText: Every Scout carries a first-aid kit. Build your own. Then show how to use each item.

lines: Every Scout can carry a small first-aid kit.
Bandages and tape cover cuts. Moleskin is a soft pad for blisters.
Ointment goes on small cuts. Gauze pads press on bleeding.
Gloves keep germs off your hands. Pick latex-free ones, in case of allergies.
A mouth barrier is a small shield for rescue breaths. Germ-killing wipes clean skin.
Do not pack candy, hair gel, or matches. They do not help with first aid.

params.title: Build Your First-Aid Kit
kidSteps: Get a quart-size bag or small pouch and label it.
Add items like bandages and ointment.
Show your leader what each item is for.
Show how to use each item correctly.
params.parentNote: A basic kit: adhesive bandages, moleskin, first-aid ointment, and latex-free gloves. Optional extras: gauze, tape, soap, scissors, mouth barrier, antiseptic wipes, pencil and paper. Check for allergies to adhesive or ointment before use.

adventures.name: Duty to God
adventures.summary: Talk about faith with your family. Meet a helper in your community. Think about what duty to God means to you.

requirements.adultText: Talk with a parent or guardian about the faith traditions your family follows, or another tradition you pick. Choose a value from it that ties to the Scout Law and discuss how each family member shows it.
requirements.kidText: Faith is what your family believes and does together. A value is something important to you, like kindness. Pick one that fits the Scout Law.

params.title: Family Faith Talk
kidSteps: Choose a time to talk with your parent or guardian.
Talk about your family's faith, or one you choose.
Pick one value from it that fits a Scout Law point.
Ask how each family member shows that value.
params.parentNote: Scouting America is nonsectarian, so any faith or belief tradition fits, and families lead this talk at home. Look for the Scout naming one value and linking it to a Scout Law point.

requirements.adultText: Meet someone from a local faith-based group that helps people in crisis whatever their beliefs. Find out who the group serves and what help it gives.
requirements.kidText: Some faith groups help anyone in a hard time. Meet someone from one in your town. Ask who they help and how.

params.title: Meet a Community Helper
kidSteps: Ask your parent or leader to help you find a local group.
Set up a visit or call with someone who works there.
Ask who they help and how they help.
Ask if they help people of any faith.
params.parentNote: Examples might include a food pantry or a shelter. A guest speaker visiting the den is one official option. Sit in on the meeting with your Scout.

requirements.adultText: Share with a parent, guardian, or adult leader how you understand Duty to God and how it shows up in your daily life.
requirements.kidText: Duty to God means following the teachings of your faith and respecting what others believe. Tell an adult what it means to you.

lines: Duty to God means following your own faith and respecting others' beliefs.
Scouting America is nonsectarian. That means it is not tied to one faith.
Scouts from every faith can join. They respect each other.
One Scout Law point is reverent. A reverent Scout is faithful to their own faith.
A reverent Scout also respects what other people believe.
Example: a friend prays in a different way than you. You respect it.

params.title: What Duty to God Means to Me
kidSteps: Pick an adult to talk with: a parent, guardian, or Scout leader.
Tell what duty to God means to you.
Share ways you live it every day.
params.parentNote: Scouting America is nonsectarian. Any faith or belief tradition fits. Let your Scout speak first and listen without correcting.

questions.prompt: Scouting America is nonsectarian. What does that mean?
choices: It is not tied to one faith
It has no rules about belief
questions.explain: Nonsectarian means open to every faith. Scouts respect each other's beliefs.

questions.prompt: Which Scout Law point is about your faith and respecting what others believe?
questions.explain: A Scout is reverent. That includes respecting the beliefs of others.

adventures.name: Citizenship
adventures.summary: Plan a safe service project. Then help your community for at least two hours.

requirements.adultText: Think of a way your group of Scouts could help the community through a service project, then use the SAFE Checklist to build a plan for doing it safely.
requirements.kidText: Think of a service project your team could do. Then use the SAFE Checklist to plan it. SAFE is a list of four safety checks.

lines: SAFE is a checklist of four safety checks for a project.
S is Supervision. Trained adults are in charge.
A is Assessment. Think about what could go wrong, and check the rules.
F is Fitness and Skill. Health records show who can take part. Each Scout needs the skill.
E is Equipment and Environment. Tools must be the right size and safe. The work area must be too.
Example: raking leaves. Who is in charge? Are the rakes the right size?

params.title: Plan a Safe Service Project
kidSteps: Think of a project that helps your community.
Write down the steps to get it done.
Check each SAFE point: Supervision, Assessment, Fitness and Skill, Equipment and Environment.
Change the plan or pick a new project if any point is unsafe.
params.parentNote: The project does not have to be carried out for real. Use the SAFE Service Project Planning Checklist and help your Scout think through all four points. If one cannot be met, choose a different project.

params.prompt: Which SAFE point does each question belong to?

items.label: Are the adults trained and trustworthy?
What could go wrong, and how do we avoid it?
Do health records show everyone can take part?
Does each Scout have the skill for the job?
Are the tools the right size and safe?
Is the work area safe in this weather?

requirements.notes: Kept as a field mission (digital false) because the Scout must name and plan a real project; the in-game sort only rehearses the four SAFE points.

requirements.adultText: Serve in a community service project for at least two hours total, either in one project or in several that add up to two hours.
requirements.kidText: Time to serve! Help out until you have put in two hours. You can add up several short projects.

params.title: Serve Your Community
kidSteps: Pick a service project with your den or your family.
Follow your safety plan.
Serve for two hours in total. Shorter projects can add up.
Tell your parent what you did and how it helped.
params.parentNote: Keep a simple log of the date, project, and time. Official options include council and national events as well as projects your den picks. Adults supervise, and tools must fit the Scout's age.

adventures.name: Outdoor Adventurer
adventures.summary: Learn the Scout Basic Essentials and plan a campout. Pack, set up camp, and go camping with your team or a troop.

requirements.adultText: Get to know the Scout Basic Essentials, the gear Scouts carry to be ready outdoors.
requirements.kidText: The Scout Basic Essentials are gear every Scout carries outside. Find them on the trail. Learn why each one matters.

lines: The Scout Basic Essentials are gear you carry on every trip outside.
Rain gear, extra clothes, and sun protection keep you dry, warm, and safe.
Trail food gives you energy. Carry at least a quart of water.
A flashlight, a map and compass, and a first-aid kit help when things go wrong.
Earn Knife Safety before you carry a pocketknife. Use matches only with an adult.
A backpack carries all of it. Find all 11 on the trail!

params.prompt: Find the Scout Basic Essentials on the trail.

targets.label: Pocketknife
targets.hint: A handy tool. You must earn Knife Safety before you carry one.

targets.label: Rain gear
targets.hint: A poncho or parka keeps you dry and blocks wind.

targets.label: Trail food
targets.hint: Granola or nuts give you energy on the trail.

targets.label: Flashlight
targets.hint: Light for the dark. Pack spare batteries.

targets.label: Extra clothing
targets.hint: Layers help when the weather changes.

targets.label: First-aid kit
targets.hint: For blisters, small cuts, and other small hurts.

targets.label: Sun protection
targets.hint: Sunscreen, a hat, and sunglasses guard your skin.

targets.label: Map and compass
targets.hint: They show the way in new places.

targets.label: Matches and fire starters
targets.hint: Use them only with training and an adult.

targets.label: Water bottle
targets.hint: Carry at least one quart of water.

requirements.notes: Eleven targets: the ten essentials plus the backpack that carries them. Hints are the teaching text. Safe to spread across the zone and reveal in two or three groups.

requirements.adultText: Work out what gear goes on an overnight camping trip, including shelter and sleeping equipment, and how it will be carried.
requirements.kidText: What would you bring on a campout? Pack the right gear in your bag. Leave out what you do not need.

lines: On a campout, you pack what keeps you warm, dry, and safe.
A tent is your shelter. A sleeping bag and pad keep you warm at night.
A backpack carries it all. Pack extra clothes and rain gear.
Bring a water bottle and a flashlight for the dark.
Leave out stuff you do not need, like a skateboard or a bowling ball.
Heavy things, like a toolbox, make your pack hard to carry.

params.prompt: Pack your bag for an overnight campout.

requirements.notes: Planning requirement, so digital. The real packing happens when the Scout prepares for the campout in requirement 5.

requirements.adultText: Go over the four points of the SAFE Checklist and how each one applies to your campout: supervision, assessment of risk, fitness and skill, and equipment and environment.
requirements.kidText: SAFE is a checklist that keeps Scouts safe. Each letter is one safety check. Show what you know about it.

lines: SAFE is a checklist that helps Scouts stay safe on a campout.
S is Supervision. Trained adults are in charge and set the example.
A is Assessment. Leaders check the risks and the rules while planning.
F is Fitness and Skill. Health records and skills show everyone can take part safely.
E is Equipment and Environment. Check your gear, the weather, and the place.
Example: you test your flashlight and check the weather. That is E.

questions.prompt: What does the S in SAFE stand for?
questions.explain: S is Supervision. Trained, trustworthy adults set the example for safety.

questions.prompt: Which SAFE point means checking for risks while planning?
questions.explain: A is Assessment. Leaders check the risks and the rules before you start.

questions.prompt: Checking health records and skills fits which point?
questions.explain: F is Fitness and Skill. Everyone must be able to take part safely.

questions.prompt: Checking the weather and testing your gear fits which point?
questions.explain: E is Equipment and Environment. Check your gear and the place. Weather can change.

requirements.adultText: Find the place where you will camp on a map, either a paper map or a digital one.
requirements.kidText: Maps show where you are going. Find your real campsite on a map. Practice map reading in the game first.

lines: A map is a picture of a place, seen from above.
A trailhead sign is where a trail starts. You begin there.
Then you follow the marker, one stop at a time.
In the game, go to the Trailhead sign, the Footbridge, and the Lookout rock.
The last stop is your Campsite.
At a real park, find camp on the map. Then trace your path.

params.title: Find Camp on the Map
kidSteps: Learn where your campout will be.
Open a paper map or a digital map.
Find the campsite and point to it.
Trace the route you will take to get there.
params.parentNote: Either a paper map or a digital map works. Help your Scout find the actual campground and talk about the route.

params.prompt: Follow the map marker to reach camp.

requirements.adultText: Join an overnight camping trip, either with your own patrol or alongside a Scouting America troop.
requirements.kidText: Time to camp! Go on a real campout with your team or a troop of older Scouts. Stay with your buddy and follow the safety rules.

params.title: Go Camping
kidSteps: Pack your gear from your list.
Go on the campout with your team or a troop.
Stay with a buddy and follow the adults' safety rules.
Help your team and have fun.
params.parentNote: Cub Scout campouts need at least one BALOO-trained adult, current Annual Health and Medical Records, and the Hazardous Weather training. A Scout camping with a troop follows Arrow of Light camping rules.

requirements.adultText: Survey the campsite and choose spots for cooking, eating, sleeping tents, and the fire ring. Put up shared patrol equipment before pitching your personal tent.
requirements.kidText: Pick smart spots for the kitchen, eating area, tents, and fire pit. Set up shared team gear first. Then put up your own tent.

lines: A good campsite is safe, flat, and set up in the right order.
Tents go on flat ground with no rocks or sticks. Stay away from dead branches.
A dry creek bed can flood. A lone tree can get hit by lightning.
Put the kitchen near water for cleanup. Never cook inside a tent.
Use the fire ring that is already there. Do not make a new one.
Set up shared team gear first. Then put up your own tent.

params.title: Set Up Camp
kidSteps: Walk around the campsite with your team.
Choose spots for the kitchen, eating area, tents, and fire pit.
Help set up the shared team gear first.
Then set up your own tent.
params.parentNote: Good tent spots are flat, free of rocks and sticks, and away from dead branches. The kitchen should be covered and near water for cleanup. Use an existing fire pit with tents a safe distance away.

ingredients.label: Shared team gear goes up first

distractors.label: Tent in a dry creek bed

requirements.adultText: Explain how to store food safely and keep the camp kitchen clean, then show it during the campout, including handwashing and dish cleanup.
requirements.kidText: Dirty hands and warm food can make people sick. Learn the rules for safe food and a clean kitchen. Then show them at camp.

lines: Germs grow on food and dirty hands. They can make people sick.
Wash your hands, then use sanitizer, before you touch food.
Meat, cheese, and eggs stay in a closed ice chest, so germs do not grow.
Use a clean board after cutting raw meat. Germs can hop onto other food.
Wash dishes in three tubs. Tub one is hot and soapy. Tub two is a hot rinse.
Tub three is cold water with sanitizer. Dump dishwater far from streams and lakes.

params.title: Keep a Clean Kitchen
kidSteps: Wash your hands, then use sanitizer, before touching food.
Keep cold foods in a closed ice chest.
Wash a board or knife from raw meat before you use it again.
Wash dishes in three tubs: soapy, rinse, then sanitizer.
Dump dishwater far from streams and lakes.
params.parentNote: Official guidance: handwashing plus sanitizer; meat, dairy, and eggs stay cold in a closed ice chest; avoid cross-contamination; three-tub washing (hot soapy, hot rinse, cold sanitizer); dump wash water about 200 feet from water sources. Check allergies first.

questions.prompt: Which foods stay in the cold ice chest?
questions.explain: Meat, dairy, and eggs must stay cold so germs do not grow.

questions.prompt: Why use a clean board after cutting raw meat?
choices: Germs can spread to other food
questions.explain: Germs can hop from raw meat onto other food and make you sick.

questions.prompt: What should you do before touching food?
questions.explain: Clean hands keep germs out of the food.

questions.prompt: What goes in the third tub when washing dishes?
questions.explain: Tub one is hot and soapy. Tub two is a hot rinse. Tub three has sanitizer.

requirements.adultText: Hold a debrief with your patrol after the campout. Share successes and ideas to improve, and point out how the group lived out Leave No Trace Principles for Kids and the Outdoor Code.
requirements.kidText: Leave No Trace means leaving nature as you found it. After camp, talk with your team. Share what worked and what to change.

lines: Leave No Trace means leaving nature the way you found it.
Pack out all your trash. Never burn it in the fire.
Stay on the trail. Do not make a new shortcut.
Leave rocks and flowers where you find them. Never carve your name in a tree.
Keep a safe distance from wildlife. Never feed the squirrels.
Use the fire ring that is already there.

params.title: Campout Wrap-Up
kidSteps: Gather your team after the campout.
Share what went well.
Share what you would change next time.
Tell how your team followed Leave No Trace.
params.parentNote: One official activity is Start, Stop, Continue: each Scout names one thing to start, stop, and continue. Use the Outdoor Code and Leave No Trace Principles for Kids as prompts.

params.prompt: Which choices follow Leave No Trace?

items.label: Leave rocks and flowers where you find them
Keep a safe distance from wildlife
Carve your name in a tree

electives.name: Champions for Nature AOL
electives.summary: See how farming and food change the planet. Find ways to waste less and help nature.

electives.name: Cycling
electives.summary: Check your bike and safety gear, then get ready for a longer bike ride.

electives.name: Engineer
electives.summary: Think like an engineer and try your own design and building projects.

electives.name: Estimations
electives.summary: Learn easy ways to guess time, height, and cost. Use them when you do not need an exact answer.

electives.name: Fishing
electives.summary: Plan a safe fishing trip. Use SAFE, a list of four safety checks.

electives.name: High Tech Outdoors
electives.summary: See how new gear and digital tools help you explore, learn, and stay safe.

electives.name: Into the Wild
electives.summary: Meet the mammals, birds, reptiles, frogs, and insects that share your neighborhood.

electives.name: Into the Woods
electives.summary: Explore the trees and plants near you and learn why they matter.

electives.name: Knife Safety
electives.summary: Learn the safety rules for pocketknives and kitchen knives. You earn the right to use a knife.

electives.name: Paddle Craft
electives.summary: Try paddling a canoe or kayak on calm water with trained adult leaders.

electives.name: Race Time AOL
electives.summary: Design and build a Pinewood Derby car or Raingutter Regatta boat. Help younger Scouts too.

electives.name: Summertime Fun AOL
electives.summary: Join three Cub Scout events this summer, like camp or a picnic.

electives.name: Swimming
electives.summary: Try the Scouting America swimmer test to get ready for water fun in Scouts BSA.
